portion_doctrine: Segments 1-10 contain a mostly intact 2Bobs podcast episode (Mar 11) on pricing strategy, specifically on option architecture and risk transfer. The episode is a deep conversation between David Baker and Blair Enns on the 'Power of Options' - how to structure 3-option proposals not as scope-escalation but as 3 distinct risk-transfer models. The first 2000 lines are webpage boilerplate (cookie banners, navigation, link lists from Pricing Creativity/Value Pricing canon); core episode starts ~line 100 and continues through segment 10. This is real, actionable content on Blair's pricing philosophy and a critical correction to how most practitioners misapply the 'good/better/best' framework.
operating_rules: Three options is the sweet spot for proposals (not two, not five+) - four is acceptable; five triggers paradox of choice
Options are NOT just different-sized buckets of deliverables/scope - that's the 'lowest expression'
Options must represent three DIFFERENT WAYS OF WORKING TOGETHER (different risk structures, engagement models)
Highest expression: three options = three distinct ways to engage at three distinct price points with fundamentally different risk allocation
Extremeness aversion principle: when given 3+ options, buyers avoid both extremes and retreat to the middle option
Price anchoring: lead with highest price option first (not to sell it, but to make other options appear affordable by comparison)
Anchoring makes the middle option the 'safe' psychological choice and increases average selected price
Value is entirely subjective and contextual - seller who controls the context controls perceived value
Three things you can sell: (1) Inputs (time/materials), (2) Outputs (deliverables/scope), (3) Outcomes (value created)
Each pricing model pushes different amounts of risk to different parties: inputs = all risk to client; outputs = shared; outcomes = more risk to provider
Context is the weapon - if you don't provide comparison/context in your proposal, the buyer will go get it elsewhere (competitor bids, mental comparisons, etc.)
Decision framing shift: proposal with one option asks client 'Is this worth X?'; proposal with three options reframes to 'Which of these is best value?'
Behavioral psychology term: 'choice architecture' or 'nudging' - the way you structure choices influences decisions

named_methods.Three-Option Proposal Architecture: Structure proposals with 3 distinct options; lead with high anchor price; use extremeness aversion to push buyers toward middle option
named_methods.Starbucks Menu Example: Tall (short), Grande (medium), Venti (large) - Starbucks removed 'Short' from menu but it's still orderable, added Venti, this shifted average selection price upward to Grande
named_methods.Risk Transfer Model: Options differ not in scope alone but in how risk is allocated between vendor and client across three dimensions: inputs, outputs, outcomes
named_methods.Value Pricing Framework: Price based on outcomes/value created (e.g., 10% of revenue recaptured, not hours spent)
named_methods.Anchoring Principle: Lead with highest-priced option to psychologically lower the perceived cost of middle options

numbers.starbucks_price_shift_example: From Short/Tall/Grande averaging middle price, to Tall/Grande/Venti with average shifting to Grande
numbers.example_value_pricing: $2M lost revenue x 10% fee = $200k engagement fee tied to recapture

specific_tactics: In proposals with 3 options, always lead presentation with the highest-priced option first
Make the middle option psychologically 'safe' by flanking it with extremes
Avoid pricing all three options as just 'small/medium/large' deliverables - that's entry-level thinking
Ask discovery questions about client's business outcome (sales loss %, profit impact) to anchor value pricing
Determine how long the work will take, multiply by hourly rate, price the outputs at the higher end of that range
If facing pricing pressure, don't cut price on outputs - restructure risk model instead (move to outcome-based or hybrid)
When proposing outcome-based pricing, calculate the value recapture (e.g., $2M lost sales x desired margin recovery) as your pricing anchor
Distinguish between: (a) selling time (inputs), (b) selling deliverables (outputs), (c) selling value/profit recapture (outcomes)
For outcome pricing, decide upfront if you'll put compensation 'at risk' - higher % of value means more risk on vendor
prompts: Why do you need [deliverable]? What are you trying to accomplish? (Discovery for outcome-based pricing)
What is your annual revenue and what is the impact of your current challenge? (To quantify outcome value)
Which of these options represents the best value?" (Two different decision frames)
If we help you reclaim $2M in lost profit, would you pay us $200,000?

contradictions: Blair emphasizes he didn't invent three-option strategy but attributes to Austrian School of Economics + Ron Baker, yet credits himself with popularizing in Pricing Creativity

Segment mentions clients confuse 'high anchor' as more scope/price without risk model change, but transcript doesn't show Blair resolving HOW to operationalize risk transfer in options (remains theoretical)
David frames the problem as 'clients don't understand risk transfer,' but the actual content mostly covers pricing structure, not risk operationalization specifics
weird_gold: Starbucks deliberately removed 'Short' from the menu but kept it orderable to psychologically anchor the 'Tall' as the new minimum, shifting average selection to 'Grande'
The Austrian School insight (Carl Menger, 1905): value is entirely subjective and contextual, not absolute - so the seller controlling the context controls value perception
The phrasing shift is critical: 'Is this worth $X?' (forces research/alternatives) vs. 'Which is best value?' (buys within your frame)
Paradox of choice hits at 5 options, not 4 - three options is mathematically + psychologically optimal
Time-based pricing (inputs) puts 100% risk on buyer; outcome pricing puts risk on seller; outputs split it - but the proposal doesn't usually articulate this
The 'coffee shop example' explains why car washes default to middle option: 3-tier menu (Bronze/Silver/Gold) triggers reflexive extremeness aversion
gates: Verify pricing framework applies to service/professional context (not product retail like Starbucks), as risk transfer mechanics differ
Confirm Blair's outcome-based pricing model includes explicit risk-sharing terms (upfront or contingent, clawbacks, etc.) - transcript doesn't detail
Check if three-option anchoring works across all buyer types or if certain ICPs (e.g., cost-conscious, high-risk-averse) reject the anchor and force competitive bids anyway
